flawed_step: Step 2 of the proof attempt. Step 1: pick a vertex v and take a Hamiltonian cycle C of G - v. Step 2: insert v into C by replacing an edge xy of C with the path x-v-y. That only works if two neighbours of v are next to each other on C. Nothing in the hypothesis makes that true, and no other choice of v or C can be shown to work in general. The step cannot be justified.
counterexample: The Petersen graph. It is connected, cubic, and has 10 vertices. It has no Hamiltonian cycle, but deleting any one vertex leaves a graph with a Hamiltonian cycle (a 9-cycle). So it is hypohamiltonian.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The natural proof (extend a Hamiltonian cycle of G - v to include v) fails because v's neighbours need not be adjacent on that cycle. Hypohamiltonian graphs are exactly the graphs where every vertex-deleted subgraph has a Hamiltonian cycle but the graph itself does not. The Petersen graph is the classic example, and it meets every stated condition: finite, simple, connected, and at least 4 vertices.
